source.title: How Do Large Language Monkeys Get Their Power (Laws)?
source.authors: Rylan Schaeffer; Joshua Kazdan; John Hughes; Jordan Juravsky; Sara Price; Aengus Lynch; Erik Jones; Robert Kirk; Azalia Mirhoseini; O. Koyejo

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling, truncation, or wrong-document issue; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes power-law behavior in success rates as inference attempts increase, not held-out pretraining loss as parameters, tokens, or training compute increase. It discusses pretraining scaling laws in its discussion but does not test them.
record.gate_note: The paper's empirical findings concern repeated-sampling inference compute and task success, a different scaling quantity from the claim versions. The distributional-estimator comparison and its synthetic-data backtest evaluate the paper's new estimator, not pretraining loss scaling, and are not recorded as claim-version results.
record.test_reason: The study analyses how success rates scale with the number of repeated inference attempts per problem (−log pass@k vs k). It does not measure held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or training compute. It does not measure downstream performance against model scale or pretraining loss, and it does not cover another training regime. Its only remark on pretraining laws is a hypothesis in the Discussion (power laws may emerge only at large compute; 'dark matter' terms), offered without any results. That makes it discussion, not a test of V1 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors show, by theorem and on reused data, that aggregate power laws in repeated sampling arise from a heavy left tail of single-attempt success rates despite per-problem exponential scaling. They show this explains Llama 3 8B IT's deviation, and that a distributional estimator recovers exponents with about an order of magnitude lower relative error. They separately conjecture that pretraining power laws may only emerge at large compute.
record.recipe_differences: This study examines repeated sampling and task success as inference attempts increase, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss across parameter, token, or training-compute scales.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that aggregate power-law behavior depends on the distribution of single-attempt success rates; Llama 3 8B IT lacks that tail and lacks aggregate power-law scaling. The authors also note that the sampling procedure for Best-of-N Jailbreaking differs from independent sampling and may account for larger differences between its two exponent estimators.

fits_no_version.finding: The mechanism behind aggregate power laws in repeated sampling. Per-problem −log success falls exponentially with k. Aggregate −log pass@k falls as a power law (b ≈ 0.19–0.37 for Pythia on MATH; 0.26–0.49 for frontier models on HarmBench) only when single-attempt success rates have a power-law left tail. Llama 3 8B IT lacks that tail and shows no aggregate power law.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repeated-sampling inference success shows aggregate power-law scaling in the number of attempts if and only if the benchmark's single-attempt success distribution has a power-law left tail, even though each problem improves exponentially.

record.problems: The empirical analyses reuse data from earlier studies rather than reporting new model runs. The text does not report uncertainty estimates for the fitted parameters, and several per-model trends are conveyed through plots alongside qualitative descriptions.
record.rows_left_out: No otherwise eligible rows were omitted. The estimator-comparison and synthetic backtesting results were left out because they assess the paper's proposed estimator rather than the pretraining-loss claims.

untested.parts: Power-law fall of held-out pretraining loss with parameters, tokens or training compute.
Extrapolating pretraining-loss fits from small to much larger runs. The estimator backtest concerns inference-attempt exponents, not runs of larger scale.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes (repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer). Repeated sampling at inference is not a training regime.
Downstream performance against model scale or pretraining loss. Table 1 lists exponents across Pythia sizes, but the paper makes no claim or analysis of scale-predictability.
Dependence of pretraining exponents on setup or fitting choices, and bending of pretraining curves. The Discussion's 'dark matter' hypothesis is conjecture with no data.

record.verdict_notes: All rows reanalyse data from Brown et al. (2024) and Hughes et al. (2024). They are refits of others' results, not new runs. Hughes et al. sampled until first success, in minibatches, so attempts were not fully independent (Appendix A). None of the rows bears on any claim version. The Discussion hypothesis about pretraining cross-entropy could be relevant background for V1/V7 bending, but it is untested.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, training tokens, and training compute.
Prediction of much larger pretraining runs from power laws fitted to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations as a function of training compute.
Effect of architecture details at fixed parameter count on pretraining loss.
Power-law behavior for pretraining loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of pretraining-loss exponents and compute-optimal allocations on setup or fitting choices, and bending of pretraining-loss curves.

rows.value: Does not exhibit power-law scaling; falls faster than any power law; no fitted a or b reported
rows.note: The paper says every prompt was successfully jailbroken within the permitted sampling budget and that the model lacks the heavy left tail associated with aggregate power-law scaling.
